# Data Methodology — Synthetic CUF Panel Generator

**This dataset is synthetic.** It is generated by `src/paimana/data/generator.py` to
mirror the structure of the real Common Upload Form (CUF) schema used by MoSPI's
PAIMANA portal, and calibrated so its portfolio-level aggregates land near
published indicative figures. It is **not** a record of real Indian infrastructure
projects. See PRD §4 for why this project treats that fact as a design constraint
to defend against, not a footnote — every dashboard screen carries a visible
banner saying so, and every quoted metric in this project is framed as evidence
about a *methodology and pipeline*, never as a claim about real-world accuracy.

This document exists so any generative choice below can be checked, argued with,
and replaced with real data through the same `paimana.data.loader.load_panel()`
socket (see §7).

---

## 1. Grain and scale

- **Grain:** one row = one project × one quarter-end snapshot (PRD §5.1). A
  single row per project cannot support an early-warning system — a warning has
  to fire *during* execution, which requires knowing what was true at
  intermediate points in time.
- **Scale (GIVEN, not assumed):** 1,981 projects, 22 sectors, a ₹150 crore
  sanctioned-cost threshold. These three come directly from the MoSPI problem
  statement.
- **Panel window:** 2006–2026 (`config.PANEL_START_YEAR` / `PANEL_END_YEAR`),
  matching the "nearly two decades of historical data" framing.
- **"Today":** fixed at `config.SIMULATION_TODAY = 2026-09-12`, not
  `datetime.today()`, so the dataset is exactly reproducible on re-generation
  regardless of when the script is actually run.

## 2. Calibration anchors — what's GIVEN vs. ASSUMED

All anchors live in `config.py` under the `ANCHOR_*` names and are checked by
`paimana.data.validate` against the generated portfolio every time
`scripts/run_validate.py` runs. Values marked ASSUMPTION are illustrative
targets, not sourced statistics — **PRD Open Item O-1** calls for verifying
them against the current published PAIMANA Flash Report. Until that happens,
changing a headline claim in this project should mean changing one constant
here, not rewriting the generator.

| Anchor | Value | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Projects | 1,981 | GIVEN |
| Sectors | 22 | GIVEN |
| Cost threshold | ₹150 crore | GIVEN |
| Share of the portfolio still ongoing (right-censored) | ~35% | ASSUMPTION |
| Share of *completed* projects with cost overrun >10% | ~20% | ASSUMPTION |
| Share of *completed* projects with time overrun >6 months | ~40% | ASSUMPTION |
| Average cost overrun among *completed* projects | ~20% | ASSUMPTION |

**Scoping note:** the overrun-share and magnitude anchors are checked on the
*completed* subset only (`is_censored == False`). This mirrors how such
published figures are actually produced — a project reports a realised overrun
once it has a final cost/date; an ongoing project reports an *anticipated*
figure, a materially different and softer signal this generator does not
attempt to reproduce.

## 3. Static project attributes (PRD §5.2)

Each project draws:
- a **sector**, weighted so land/civil-heavy sectors (Railways, Roads, Water
  Resources) are over-represented relative to smaller programme sectors
  (Textiles, Information & Broadcasting) — `_SECTOR_PROFILE` in `generator.py`;
- an **approved cost** from a log-normal distribution whose median is set per
  sector (large-infrastructure sectors skew larger);
- an **original duration** from a log-normal distribution whose median is also
  set per sector, then globally stretched by `_DURATION_SCALE_MULT = 1.75`.
  This stretch is an explicit tuning knob, not an arbitrary inflation: large
  sanctioned programmes commonly run 5–8+ years end to end, and the panel
  needs enough quarters per project to be a genuine longitudinal dataset
  rather than a handful of snapshots (see §6 for why this mattered);
- a **sanction date** drawn from a Beta(1.8, 1.6) distribution over the panel
  window, skewed toward the more recent half so a realistic share of the
  portfolio is still executing today (see §6);
- an **implementing agency**, drawn from a small sector-specific pool
  (`N_AGENCIES_PER_SECTOR = 6` per sector) so agency identity is persistent
  and meaningful — the same agency recurs across several projects, which is
  what makes an "agency's historical track record" a coherent feature for
  Phase 2 to build.

## 4. Latent risk structure

Three unobserved effects combine into one project-level **risk propensity**
(squashed to (0, 1) via a logistic transform):

1. **Sector latent risk** — a per-sector baseline (e.g. Railways and Water
   Resources run structurally riskier than Telecom or Textiles), plus noise.
2. **Agency latent skill** — a persistent per-agency effect, so some
   implementing agencies are chronically better or worse executors across all
   their projects.
3. **Project idiosyncratic noise** — the dominant term, ensuring no model can
   ever fully explain outcomes from observable attributes alone. This is
   deliberate: PRD §4.3.5 requires that the simulation NOT be trivially
   learnable, so a downstream model reporting near-perfect accuracy is treated
   as a leakage bug, not a success.

Risk propensity drives, but does not determine, everything below — every
mechanism that uses it also adds substantial independent quarter-level or
project-level noise.

## 5. Quarterly execution simulation (PRD §5.3)

Each project is simulated quarter by quarter from sanction until true
completion:

- **Physical progress** advances each quarter by a velocity built from: a
  bell-shaped construction-phase multiplier (slow–fast–slow, floored at 0.55
  so it never collapses to zero even late in a delayed project — see §6 for
  why that floor exists), a penalty from currently-active delay reasons, a
  regime-shift penalty (see below), and quarter-level noise.
- **Delay reasons** (land acquisition, forest/environmental clearance, funds
  constraint, contractor issues, tendering delay, litigation, R&R, law and
  order, geological surprise, equipment supply, statutory clearance, force
  majeure) switch on and off stochastically each quarter; onset probability
  scales with the project's risk propensity, and an active reason resolves
  with a fixed per-quarter probability. Multiple reasons can be active at
  once, each compounding the velocity penalty.
- **A regime-shift window** (`REGIME_SHIFT_YEAR = 2020`, 8 quarters) applies a
  universal, non-project-specific slowdown to every active project during
  that period — representing a generic macro disruption (not a specific
  claim about any real event), giving the panel a historically-plausible
  systemic shock rather than every quarter being independently drawn.
- **Financial progress** ("spending") is modelled as physical progress plus a
  "gap" — the classic early leading indicator where money is disbursed ahead
  of verified physical work. This gap is a genuine *feature* signal (it
  correlates with, but does not determine, the eventual outcome — see §6).
- **Missingness**: `physical_progress_pct`, `expenditure_to_date_cr`, and
  `financial_progress_pct` each get 5–12% of values independently nulled,
  simulating realistic quarterly non-reporting gaps.

## 6. Terminal outcomes and two build-time bugs this methodology corrects

Two mechanisms deliberately **decouple the mid-execution trail from the
terminal outcome**, and both exist because of concrete failures found while
calibrating this generator against the anchors in §2 (documented here rather
than only in git history, because the reasoning is part of the methodology):

**(a) The phase-multiplier floor.** An earlier version let the construction
S-curve multiplier go negative once a project passed its *original* planned
duration (elapsed time fraction > 1). Any project even slightly behind at its
deadline then saw velocity collapse toward zero — a runaway "never finishes"
spiral, observed directly as projects stuck at ~50% physical progress after
3× their planned duration. The fix freezes the phase fraction at 1.0 past the
deadline, giving a sustained (not collapsing) closing-out pace. This is why
the multiplier's floor (0.55) is load-bearing, not cosmetic.

**(b) Terminal cost is a calibrated function of portfolio-relative risk
percentile, not a running total of the quarterly "gap."** An earlier version
derived final cost directly from the last simulated quarter's frontloading
gap plus a closeout-noise multiplier. Because the gap's mean was structurally
non-negative, nearly every completed project came out overrun (88% vs. the
~20% anchor), while a separate bug meant many projects were actually captured
mid-crawl at ~60% financial progress, producing a *negative* aggregate mean.
Once (a) was fixed, direct tuning of the gap/closeout formulas still could not
hit both the overrun **share** (~20%) and the overrun **average magnitude**
(~20%) at once with a single symmetric noise term — those two moments only
coexist under a right-skewed distribution (most projects finish near budget,
a risk-weighted minority blows out by a large multiple), which a linear or
mildly-nonlinear function of risk propensity could not produce given the
generator's actual risk-propensity population (empirically mean 0.54, std
0.14 — a narrow effective range).

The fix: compute each project's **rank percentile** of risk propensity within
the whole 1,981-project portfolio, and map that percentile through a highly
convex function (`-10 + 600 * percentile**18`, plus independent quarter-level
noise, std 6) before drawing the final cost. Only the top slice of the
portfolio's risk ranking produces large overruns; the rest cluster near
budget. Coefficients were fit by direct Monte Carlo against the actual
generated risk-percentile population (not derived analytically) to land the
overrun share and the overrun average simultaneously inside their tolerance
bands — see the Phase 1 Handoff Report in `HANDOFF.md` for the calibration
trace. The mid-execution "gap" feature is retained unchanged as a genuine but
imperfect *leading indicator*: a project can look frontloaded and still close
out near budget, which is realistic and is exactly the kind of signal a
model should have to learn probabilistically rather than read off a lookup
table.

**Time overrun**, by contrast, emerges organically from the quarter-by-quarter
simulation (no separate closed-form formula) — final duration is simply
however many quarters it actually took physical progress to reach 100%.

## 7. Censoring — why it is NOT a coin flip

A project is right-censored ("Ongoing") if its *true simulated completion
date* falls after `SIMULATION_TODAY`; otherwise it is "Completed" and its
final cost/date are revealed. This means censoring is a **consequence** of
sanction recency and simulated duration, not an independently-drawn flag —
exactly the mechanism that produces right-censoring in real survival data,
and it is what makes recently-sanctioned projects disproportionately likely
to still be "ongoing," matching the real portfolio's structure. For censored
projects, panel snapshots after `SIMULATION_TODAY` are not emitted (an
analyst monitoring today's PAIMANA portal cannot see a project's future),
and every terminal target column (`final_cost_cr`, `cost_overrun_pct`,
`y_cost_overrun`, etc.) is set to null rather than backfilled from the
generator's internal "true" outcome — revealing them would be a direct
leakage channel dressed up as ground truth.

## 8. The real-data socket

`paimana.data.loader.load_panel(source="real")` is intentionally
unimplemented. It raises `NotImplementedError` naming the exact columns
(`paimana.data.schema.STATIC_COLUMNS`, `SNAPSHOT_COLUMNS`, `TARGET_COLUMNS`)
a real CUF extract would need to provide at the grain defined in §1. Wiring in
a genuine PAIMANA export means writing one function that returns two
DataFrames matching that contract — nothing else in the pipeline changes.

## 9. Known limitations (stated plainly)

- Sector, ministry, and state names are illustrative; ministry names are
  synthesized as `"Ministry of {sector}"` rather than drawn from the real
  government structure.
- The regime-shift window is a generic macro-disruption proxy, not a claim
  about any specific historical event.
- Delay-reason base rates and the risk-propensity → outcome mapping are
  fitted to hit the §2 anchors, not derived from any published root-cause
  breakdown of Indian infrastructure delays.
- All of the above are exactly why every metric this project reports is
  framed as *"a validated methodology, benchmarked on data calibrated to
  published aggregates"* (PRD §4.3.3) — never as a real-world accuracy claim.
